newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU pins competitive hopes on single currency.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU pins competitive hopes on single currency.

text.p: Monetary union will boost the competitiveness of the 15-nation European Union which is lagging behind rival economic superpowers the United States and Japan, the European Commission said on Wednesday.
"The creation of economic and monetary union (EMU) will have a positive effect on competitiveness," Industrial Affairs Commissioner Martin Bangemann told a news conference.

But the senior German commissioner a the EU executive said countries which choose to stay outside the single currency when it starts in 1999 would suffer economically, for example in terms of higher capital costs.
A Commission report analysing the "poor" competitive performance of Europe's industry said EMU would help industry to take full advantage of the bloc's single market.
It would also lower transaction costs of cross-border payments and the single currency, the euro, may become an international currency in the same way as the dollar.
Bangemann stressed the need for a stable single currency, saying its value should not be used as a "competitive tool".
"The important thing is that a stable currency will be able to fit in better into world trade than an inflationary one."
Apart from the optimistic assessment of the impact of EMU, the Commission report presented by Bangemann painted a largely negative picture of the continent's competitive strength.

"The Commission has found that Europe's industry is lagging behind behind major competitors like the United States and Japan, in terms of job creation, productivity levels and employment rates," a Commission statement said.
As a result, the EU level of gross domestic product (GDP) per capita is nearly one third below that of the United States and one sixth less than Japan.

High costs and low investment have combined to depress Europe's industrial performance, it said. Public deficits are too high, spending on research insufficient and the adoption of new technologies remain too slow.
"Export market shares, profit margins and investment returns remain inadequate," the Commission said.

"High levels of costs of key inputs such as labour, energy, water, communications and transport, and low investment in research and development, plants and equipment contribute to EU industry's poor performance," it added.
In spite of much improved economic fundamentals, European industry has not been performing as well as it might.
"The situation of European industry...is not satisfactory," Bangemann said. "Only by means of innovation will we be able to gain on the competitiveness front in the long term."
Lack of flexibility on the labour market was also a key factor in Europe's disappointing performance.

The EU -- grouping the most developed industrial countries in Europe -- has seen its share of export markets in the 28-nation Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development decline since 1987, Bangemann said.
Since 1960, the EU has mananged to create only 10 million new jobs, half the number generated in Japan and less than a fifth of those in the United States.
As a result, the EU unemployment rate stands at almost 11 percent of the workforce, twice as high as in the United States and three times more than in Japan.
"Of the manufacturing sectors, only food, drink, and tobacco and wood and furniture grew faster in the European Union than in the United States and Japan between 1985 and 1995," it said.
